passages.title: The Oil Lamp Room
passages.text:
Welcome to the Oil Lamp Room!

Before electricity, people needed light after dark. For thousands of years, they used small oil lamps like the ones in this room.

How were the lamps made? First, a potter shaped wet clay by hand or pressed it into a mould. Next, the lamp dried in the sun for a few days. Then it was baked in a very hot oven. At home, people filled the lamp with olive oil and put a thin piece of cloth in the small hole at the front. They lit the cloth, and it burned slowly for hours.

Look at the lamps in Case 3. Some of them have pictures of birds, fish and plants on top. These lamps were more expensive.

Please do not touch the lamps. They are very old and break easily. Children can make their own clay lamp at the activity table near the exit.

passages.title: Beach Clean-Up Day
passages.text:
Volunteers wanted! Do you love the sea? Then come and help us keep it clean!

When: Friday, 14 June, 8:00 to 11:00 a.m.
Where: North Beach, next to the lifeguard tower

Last summer, 60 volunteers collected more than 200 kilos of rubbish from the sand, most of it plastic bottles and bottle caps. This year we want to do even better.

We will give every volunteer gloves, a bag and a cold drink. Bring a hat, sun cream and a water bottle. Please wear closed shoes, because there may be broken glass on the sand.

Volunteers aged 12 to 15 must come with an adult. Groups from schools and youth movements are welcome.

It is the best way to start a summer weekend, and you will meet great people! To join, send a message with your name and age to the Green Coast Club before 10 June.

passages.title: My First Practice
passages.text:
Hi Yael,

How are you? I have big news: I joined a basketball team! You know I always played in the park with my brother, but this is my first real team.

On Monday I went to my first practice. I was really nervous. First, the coach asked us to run around the court ten times. After that, we practised passing in pairs. My partner was a tall girl called Shira. She plays very well, but she was patient with me. At the end, we played a short game. I didn't score any points, but I made two good passes.

The team practises twice a week, on Mondays and Thursdays. Our first match is next month, against a team from Haifa. I don't know if the coach will let me play, but I'm going to practise every day.

Can you come and watch the match? It would be so cool to see you there!

Love,
Noa

passages.title: Rare Flowers Return
passages.text:
Hundreds of purple irises are blooming on Oren Hill this month, for the first time in five years.

These flowers need a lot of rain. In the last few winters there was very little rain, so only a few irises grew. This winter was much wetter, and now the hill is full of colour.

Last week, a class of eighth-grade students from the local school walked up the hill with a park ranger. First, the ranger showed them how to walk only on the path. Then the students counted the flowers. They found 412 irises. In the end, they shared their results on the school website.

"It was the most beautiful trip of the year," said Amir, one of the students.

The ranger asks visitors not to pick the flowers. "If you pick an iris, it cannot make seeds for next year," she explained. Visitors can see the flowers until the end of March.

passages.title: How to Make a Bottle Bird Feeder
passages.text:
In winter, it is harder for small birds to find food. You can help them with a simple feeder made from an old plastic bottle.

You need: an empty plastic bottle with its cap, two wooden spoons, a piece of string and some bird seed.

1. Wash the bottle and let it dry. Wet seeds go bad quickly.
2. Ask an adult to make two pairs of small holes in the bottle, one pair near the bottom and one pair in the middle.
3. Push a wooden spoon through each pair of holes. Birds will stand on the spoons.
4. Ask the adult to cut a bigger hole just above the end of each spoon. The seeds will come out here.
5. Fill the bottle with seeds and close the cap.
6. Tie the string around the top of the bottle and hang the feeder from a tree branch.

Now wait a few days. Birds are careful, and they need time to trust something new. Remember to add more seeds every week!

passages.title: Three Chords and a Lot of Patience
passages.text:
When I turned fifteen, my grandfather gave me his old guitar. It had been sitting in his cupboard for thirty years, and two of the strings were missing. I bought new strings online and watched a video about how to put them on. It took me a whole evening, but when I finally played a note, it sounded almost like real music.

Then the hard part started. My fingers hurt after only ten minutes of practice, and I couldn't press the strings hard enough. A teacher at the community centre told me this happens to everyone. "Play for fifteen minutes every day," she said, "not two hours once a week." I followed her advice, and after about three weeks the pain went away.

Now, two months later, I know three chords: G, C and D. That doesn't sound like much, but you can play hundreds of songs with just those three. Last Friday I played a simple song for my grandfather. He sang along, and I think he enjoyed it more than any present I have ever given him.

In my opinion, learning an instrument is the best thing a teenager can do with free time. It is much more satisfying than scrolling through videos. If you are thinking about starting, my advice is simple: be patient with your fingers, and don't give up in the first month.

passages.title: Under the Desert Sky
passages.text:
Lior Shani, 24, leads night tours in the Negev desert, where people come to look at the stars. We asked him about the job.

Why the desert?
Light from cities hides the stars. Here, far from big towns, the sky is really dark. On a clear night, you can see thousands of stars with your own eyes, and the Milky Way looks like a river of light.

How did you start?
When I was twelve, my school took us on a trip to an observatory. Afterwards, I saved money for two years to buy my first small telescope. Later I studied physics at university, and during my studies I started working as a guide at weekends.

What happens on a tour?
First, we walk a few minutes away from the cars, and everyone turns off their phone screens. It takes about twenty minutes for your eyes to get used to the dark. Then I point out planets and stars with a green laser. At the end, people look through a big telescope.

What is your favourite moment?
When someone sees the rings of Saturn for the first time. Adults scream like children! Honestly, I think it is the most amazing sight in the universe.

Any advice for young stargazers?
You don't need expensive equipment. Lie on a blanket, let your eyes rest, and just look up.

passages.title: The Woman Who Listened to Bats
passages.text:
This is a made-up story. Leah Doron was born in 1951 in a small village in the Galilee. As a child, she spent summer evenings on the roof of her house, watching bats fly over the fields. Most of her neighbours were afraid of them, but Leah wanted to know how they found insects in the dark.

After finishing school, Leah served in the army and then studied biology. In 1978 she visited a cave in the Judean Desert for the first time. There she counted more than two thousand bats sleeping upside down. She later said that this day changed her life.

Bats find food by making very high sounds and listening for the echo. Humans cannot hear these sounds. In the 1980s, Leah built a small machine that turned bat calls into sounds that people could hear. With it, she discovered that different kinds of bats "speak" in different ways.

Her work also showed that bats help farmers, because a single bat can eat hundreds of insects in one night. Thanks to her reports, several caves were closed to visitors to protect the animals.

Leah taught at a university for thirty years and wrote two books for children about bats. When she retired, she said, "People fear what they don't understand." Today, many young scientists continue her research. In my view, she was one of the most important nature scientists of her generation.

passages.title: Game Review: Pocket Planet
passages.text:
Pocket Planet is a new phone game in which you look after a tiny world. At the start, your planet is just grey rock. You add water, plants and animals, and you watch how they affect each other. If you add too many rabbits, they eat all the grass. If you add foxes, the number of rabbits goes down again.

The game was made by a team of four students as a university project, and it is free to download. There are no adverts, which is rare for a free game. You can play without an internet connection, so it is perfect for long bus rides.

What I liked most was how much I learned without noticing. After a week, I understood food chains better than after a whole term of biology lessons. The graphics are simple but charming, and the calm music is lovely.

However, the game has some problems. The instructions are too short, so for the first hour I had no idea what to do. Also, once your planet is balanced, there is not much left to do. I finished all twenty levels in about ten days.

Overall, Pocket Planet is a clever and relaxing game. It is not perfect, but I would recommend it to anyone who likes nature or puzzles, especially younger players who want to learn something while they play.

Rating: 4 out of 5

passages.title: The Broken String
passages.text:
The hall was full. Maya could see her parents in the third row, and her little brother was waving a paper sign with her name on it. She sat down, put the violin under her chin and looked at the conductor.

The youth orchestra had practised this piece for four months. Maya had a short solo in the middle, only sixteen bars, but she had dreamed about it every night for a week.

The music began, and the first part went perfectly. Then, just four bars before her solo, Maya heard a sharp sound, like a small whip. Her E string, the thinnest one, had broken. It hung from the violin like a piece of hair.

For a second, she could not breathe. Everyone would hear her fail. Then she felt a gentle touch on her arm. Daniel, the boy sitting next to her, was holding out his own violin. Without a word, he took hers and put it on his knees.

Maya lifted Daniel's violin. It felt heavier than hers, and the strings were a little different. She closed her eyes and played.

When the solo ended, she opened her eyes. The conductor was smiling at her, and in the third row her mother was wiping her eyes.

After the concert, Maya found Daniel by the door. "You didn't play the last part," she said. "You gave up your own music for me."

He shrugged. "Sixteen bars," he said. "That's nothing between friends."

passages.title: Fix It, Don't Bin It
passages.text:
Last year my headphones stopped working. One side went silent, and I did what most people my age would do: I threw them away and ordered a new pair. A week later, my uncle, who repairs old radios as a hobby, asked to see the broken ones. I dug them out of the rubbish bin. He opened them with a tiny screwdriver, found a loose wire and fixed it in under ten minutes. I was embarrassed, and I have been thinking about it ever since.

We live surrounded by machines we do not understand. According to a United Nations report, the world produced around 62 million tonnes of electronic waste in 2022, and less than a quarter of it was recorded as properly collected and recycled. Much of that waste is not broken beyond repair; it is simply broken beyond our knowledge.

This is why I believe every secondary school should run a weekly repair club. Students would bring in broken lamps, toys, bicycles and phones, and volunteers from the community, such as retired electricians, tailors and engineers, would show them how to fix them. Some towns already run "repair cafés" like this for adults, and many of them are popular.

Critics will say that schools are already too busy and that repair is a job for professionals. They have a point: nobody should open a microwave oven without training. But a repair club is not about turning teenagers into technicians. It is about confidence. A student who has replaced a bicycle chain or sewn on a button learns that objects are not magic boxes, and that problems can often be solved with patience.

Besides, the skills are surprisingly useful in other subjects. Physics becomes real when you follow an electric current with your own hands.

My headphones still work, by the way. Every time I put them on, I hear a small reminder: before you throw something away, open it up.

passages.title: The Busiest Sky in the World
passages.text:
Twice a year, something remarkable happens above Israel. Every year, an estimated 500 million birds pass over this narrow strip of land: they fly south in autumn and north again in spring. But why do so many birds choose this route?

The answer is geography. Many birds spend the summer in Europe and western Asia, where they build nests and raise their young. When the weather turns cold and insects become hard to find, they fly south to spend the winter in Africa. In spring, they make the same journey in the opposite direction.

Large birds such as storks, pelicans and eagles face a special problem. Flapping their huge wings for hours would use too much energy, so they glide instead. To do this, they need thermals: columns of warm air that rise when the sun heats the ground. A stork circles inside a thermal and climbs high without moving its wings. Then it glides forward, slowly losing height, until it finds the next thermal.

Thermals form over land, but hardly at all over the sea, because water heats up slowly. As a result, soaring birds avoid long flights over the Mediterranean. Instead, they travel around its eastern end, where the land bridge between Asia and Africa forces them into a narrow corridor. Israel sits right in the middle of that corridor.

This creates challenges as well as wonders. In the past, large flocks were a serious danger to aircraft, and several planes were damaged in collisions with birds. Today, researchers track the flocks with radar and send warnings to pilots, so such accidents are much less common.

Next time you see a long, shining line of storks circling over a field, remember that some of them may have started their trip in Poland and could end it in South Africa.

passages.title: Teen Volunteers Uncover Ancient Mosaic
passages.text:
This news story is made up, but finds like it are real. A colourful mosaic floor, believed to be about 1,600 years old, has been uncovered by teenage volunteers during a summer excavation in the Lower Galilee, archaeologists announced on Monday.

The discovery was made by chance. The group of 35 volunteers, aged 16 to 18, had been digging for two weeks at the site of an ancient farming village. On the last Thursday of the dig, 17-year-old Noam Katz was cleaning soil from the bottom of a stone wall when his brush touched small coloured stones. "At first I thought it was just gravel," he said. "Then I saw a red line, and then the shape of a bird's wing."

The archaeologists immediately stopped all other work in that area. Over the following four days, the team carefully removed the soil with brushes and small tools. The floor, which measures about six metres by four, shows birds, grapes and a large vase surrounded by vines.

According to Dr. Ronit Efrat, who directs the excavation, the floor probably belonged to the house of a wealthy family, or perhaps to a public building. "We will only know after we study the whole structure," she said. "Either way, it is one of the finest mosaics found in this region in the past decade."

The mosaic has now been photographed and covered with a protective layer of cloth and sand to keep it safe from sun and rain. Experts will decide next year whether to move it to a museum or to protect it where it was found.

The volunteer programme, which has run every summer since 2015, gives young people a chance to experience real archaeological work. Its organisers say this year's discovery shows that anyone can make history, sometimes with nothing more than a paintbrush.

passages.title: Do You Really Need 10,000 Steps?
passages.text:
For years, my watch buzzed happily every evening when I reached 10,000 steps. If I had only managed 9,000, I would walk around the living room until the number changed. I was sure that 10,000 was a scientific target. It turns out that it is not.

The number seems to have started with marketing, not medicine. In the 1960s, a company in Japan sold one of the first popular step counters, and its name meant something like "10,000-step meter". The round number was easy to remember, and it spread around the world.

Since then, scientists have actually studied the question. Several large studies, which together followed tens of thousands of adults for years, found that people who walked more did tend to live longer. However, the benefits did not keep rising at the same speed. When researchers combined the results of fifteen of these studies in 2022, they found that the extra gains became much smaller at around 6,000 to 8,000 steps a day for adults over 60, and at around 8,000 to 10,000 steps for younger adults. In other words, 10,000 is not a magic line; it is just one point on a curve.

To me, this is the most encouraging health news I have read in years. Many people give up on exercise because the goal feels impossible. If someone moves from 3,000 steps a day to 6,000, that is a real achievement, and it may bring real benefits, even if the watch does not celebrate.

Steps are also not the whole story. Experts usually recommend activities that make your heart beat faster, as well as exercises that strengthen your muscles.

So I have changed my approach. First, I turned off the evening reminder. Then I started walking to school at a faster pace, and later I added two short strength sessions a week. My step count is lower than before, but I feel fitter than ever. The best number, I have decided, is the one you can keep up.
